rationale: Recorded the tie-break receipt that completes the permutation space of the three-reply set: the three added orders behave exactly as the trigger position predicts, so the last named discriminator of this question is measured and no order contradicts the mechanism. Knowledge entry 2b0dd5bd and the recovery-value family fact gained the receipt as a citation (their statements already describe the measured rule), the interpretation gained the receipt, the completed-permutation wording and a fresh counterevidence and limitation set, and the question's discriminator was restated around the remaining unmeasured axis (reply sets whose value ballots differ or whose post-trigger replies could re-reach the quorum).

knowledge.statement: A nil command slice does not stay nil across the wire: PrepareReply.Unmarshal (and the other RPC decoders) allocate the received slice with make([]state.Command, alen1), so a sender that carries no command yields a non-nil empty slice at the receiver. In handlePrepareReply's adoption loop that empty slice is copied into lb.cmds, and the sub-case 5/6 fallback tests only `inst.lb.cmds != nil`, so it passes the empty slice to startPhase1 instead of substituting state.NOOP(); the resulting instance holds an empty (non-nil) command list, which executeCommands accepts because its guard is also a nil test, and handleCommit's re-offer path does not recognise it because that path requires exactly one command with operation NONE. Which command is adopted is the one carried by the last reply appended before len(lb.prepareReplies) reaches SlowQuorumSize; the recoverer's own fabricated reply is already appended, so with one self reply the trigger falls on the second delivered peer reply, and the dispatch hands the instance to startPhase1 with fresh bookkeeping, so replies delivered after the trigger are appended to that new bookkeeping and never enter the decision. Measured on one fixed reply set with two command-carrying and two empty peer replies, the owner's command survives exactly when the reply at that trigger position carries it - kept for the delivery orders 1,2,3,4 and 3,1,4,2, dropped for 1,3,4,2 and 3,4,1,2 - so neither the first delivered reply nor the number of command-carrying replies decides the outcome.
knowledge.conditions: Recovery whose replies include one from a replica that holds the instance with no command, when that reply's VBallot is at least the running candidate ballot (epaxos/defs.go:228-235, epaxos/epaxos.go:1239-1246, 1291-1296, 1307-1311 and 1090-1099).

knowledge.statement: In the captured EPaxos package the value a recovery adopts is not protected by the quorum that holds it: four distinct mechanisms of the same recovery path each let a recovering replica end up proposing, and then deciding, a value other than the one its prepare replies carry. (a) startRecoveryForInstance fabricates a value ballot for its own empty state, so the adoption loop skips genuine replies (epaxos/epaxos.go:1145-1165, 1239-1246). (b) A reply whose value ballot is below the running candidate ballot - which begins at the recoverer's pre-recovery local value ballot and rises to the fabricated recovery ballot as the loop adopts - is ignored even when it reports the highest accepted value, so a NOOP replaces an accepted value, including one another live replica has already committed; a reply whose value ballot equals the running candidate is still adopted, which is what lets an empty reply replace the command in (d). (c) A reply that reports the instance COMMITTED is discarded once its status reaches lb.status, because the pre-accept guard then rejects the remaining replies, so the first recovery attempt stalls until the retry (epaxos/epaxos.go:870-881, 1255-1313). (d) A reply that carries no command decodes as a non-nil empty slice, which the sub-case 5/6 fallback passes to startPhase1 instead of state.NOOP() (epaxos/defs.go:228-235, epaxos/epaxos.go:1307-1311), and the adopted value is the one carried by the last reply appended before the appended count reaches SlowQuorumSize - the fabricated self reply counts toward that threshold, so the trigger falls on the second delivered peer reply and the dispatch then replaces the bookkeeping, so replies delivered afterwards cannot restore the command; the owner's command therefore survives exactly when that second peer reply carries it, measured on one fixed reply set with two command-carrying and two empty peer replies as kept for the orders 1,2,3,4 and 3,1,4,2 and dropped for 1,3,4,2 and 3,4,1,2. Recovering replicas that already hold the value are not affected by (a)-(b), and the client re-offer protects the single-NOOP case but not the empty-slice case.
knowledge.conditions: N=5, F=2 configuration of the captured snapshot with Thrifty on and IsLeader false at the recovering replica; the instance owner fails inside its accept window and the recovering replica holds the instance without its command, or (for the arrival-order variant) recovers its own instance while replies at the same value ballot differ.

knowledge.assertion: empty slice adopted and passed through, with the reply at the slow-quorum trigger position deciding the command
COMMITTED status adopted then later replies discarded
a recovery lacking the command can decide a different value than a live replica's committed value

investigations.hypothesis: The adoption loop takes any reply whose VBallot is at least the running candidate ballot and copies its command into the candidate, so a reply at the same value ballot that carries no command can replace the command the owner itself contributed; because the fabricated self reply is already in the appended set, the dispatch fires on the second delivered peer reply, and the candidate adopted then is handed to startPhase1 (sub-case 5/6) as the instance's command, so replies delivered after the trigger are appended to the fresh bookkeeping and cannot restore the command. On one fixed reply set with two command-carrying and two empty peer replies the owner's command therefore survives exactly when the second delivered peer reply carries it: kept for the orders 1,2,3,4 and 3,1,4,2, dropped for 1,3,4,2 and 3,4,1,2. The six permutations of the three-reply set follow the same rule: 2,4,3, 3,4,2, 2,3,4 and 4,3,2 drop the command while 3,2,4 and 4,2,3 keep it, so the completed permutation space of that reply set contains no order that contradicts the mechanism.
investigations.discriminator: Whether some reply set still overrides the trigger position - a reply whose value ballot exceeds the fabricated candidate, or enough replies delivered after the trigger to re-reach SlowQuorumSize on the fresh bookkeeping, which this configuration cannot produce; both halves of the original discriminator are now measured, since the six permutations of the three-reply set and the four orders of the four-reply set all follow the trigger position and the number of command-carrying replies does not decide the outcome.

interpretations.rationale: Current account: the anomaly is resolved and it is a defect distinct from the fabricated-self-ballot one. Receipt 81a44ff62122417db3cc5697fc5303f6 (fixed experiment 0757162a4aa64ef4a58a90002641eb27-experiment) shows the owner holding its command X at status ACCEPTED before its own recovery (index 0), the empty acceptor at status NONE after the Accept (index 3), and, after the owner recovered its own instance and the three PrepareReplies were delivered, an instance left at status PREACCEPTED with an empty command list plus bookkeeping whose candidate command is an empty slice (index 4: inst_cmds_len 0, inst_status 1, lb_cmds_len 0, lb_status 1, lb_appended 1, lb_nacks 0), with no command proposed afterwards (index 5) and the same values in the second run (indices 9-11); comparison 0 and comparison 1 are both violated with witnesses 5 and 11. The mechanism is now sourced: a reply from a replica that holds no command carries a nil command slice, the decoder allocates it with make([]state.Command, alen1) so the receiver sees a non-nil empty slice (epaxos/defs.go:228-235), the adoption loop copies that empty slice into lb.cmds because its VBallot equals the running candidate ballot (epaxos/epaxos.go:1239-1246), and the sub-case 5/6 fallback substitutes state.NOOP() only when lb.cmds is nil (epaxos/epaxos.go:1307-1311), which an empty slice is not - so startPhase1 is called with an empty command batch and the instance becomes PREACCEPTED with Cmds of length zero (epaxos/epaxos.go:1291-1296, 751-779). That also explains why the probe recorded no PreAccept command (proposed_cmd_op -1 was the empty batch, not an absent proposal) and why the probe's two runs coincided: the empty slice wins in both delivery orders because the loop adopts ties with >= and the empty reply is adopted whatever its position, the last delivery being irrelevant. Consequences for the captured package: the instance is proposed and can be decided with no command at all, replacing the command the owner itself held; executeCommands accepts an empty non-nil batch because its guard is a nil test, so the instance executes as a no-op rather than stalling; and the client re-offer path that protects the fabricated-NOOP case does not fire here, because handleCommit tests for exactly one command with operation NONE (epaxos/epaxos.go:1090-1099), which an empty batch never satisfies. A second receipt measures the client-side consequence of exactly that decision: receipt 098ab4425325464192aa558be557f0ce (fixed experiment 49b316fdc67c459fb374500fb7f26514-experiment) attaches a real client proposal (command id 91) to the owner's own instance, that instance's own recovery decides the empty batch, and both declared comparisons are violated with complete witness 4 - the decided instance holds a command list of length zero while the owner held command X before (index 0: status 3, cmd_op 1) and the owner's pending request is never re-offered (requeued 0 with pending_proposals 1 and reply_bytes 0), while the single-NOOP decision of the same family (receipt 893f6180a4514a8d9e20a1d5e6698542) re-queued its request and later completed it. The contrast is the re-offer guard's own condition: handleCommit requires exactly one command with operation NONE (epaxos/epaxos.go:1090-1099), which an empty batch never satisfies, so the empty-command decision drops the client's request with neither a reply nor a re-offer. The delivery-order question is now measured with three runs of the same reply set (receipt e89ecb076e8d4a78b174f848562ed77f, fixed experiment e8fb81e1cb0742118ce33f60e08a0de1-experiment): with the replies delivered as 2,4,3 the instance ends with no command (comparison 0 violated, witness 6); as 3,4,2 the same outcome (comparison 1 violated, witness 13); and as 3,2,4 - where the command-carrying reply is the second delivered - the instance keeps the owner's command (comparison 2 holds, evaluated 20). The mechanism is therefore not a simple last-reply-wins rule over the whole set but the timing of the quorum trigger: handlePrepareReply dispatches as soon as len(lb.prepareReplies) reaches SlowQuorumSize, which for one self reply and a five-replica configuration is two peer replies, and the candidate command is whatever the last adopted reply in that prefix carries. In this reply set two peers carry no command and one carries X, so two of the three delivery orders put an empty reply in the adopted position and lose the command, while the third order puts X there and keeps it. The adopted value therefore depends on arrival order among equally admissible replies rather than on their content, and the empty-slice handling is what makes the losing orders lose the command outright instead of substituting state.NOOP(). The earlier statement that the order variant was unmeasured is withdrawn; the state/command invariant entry is qualified rather than wrong: it holds for the command-carrying writers, while this path reaches the same status-without-command combination through an empty non-nil slice, which that entry's nil test does not cover. The deciding position is now observed rather than derived, with a four-order receipt on a fixed reply set that holds two command-carrying and two empty peer replies (receipt 251562364ca64b3c80cd14e0d6aeddc3, fixed experiment e25f403842234594881914f730efff4e-experiment, test TestAssuranceEPaxosRecoveryMixedQuorumOrder, exit 0, 40 parsed events, no diagnostics). The harness reads the recoverer's leader-bookkeeping pointer before and after every delivery, so the trigger is observed as the delivery that replaces that object: in all four orders the replacement happens on the second delivered peer reply - index 5 for the order 1,2,3,4 with reply 2 carrying the command, index 15 for 1,3,4,2 with reply 3 carrying none, index 25 for 3,4,1,2 with reply 4 carrying none, index 35 for 3,1,4,2 with reply 1 carrying the command - and the fresh bookkeeping that startPhase1 installs already carries the decision (fresh_lb_ballot -1, fresh_lb_status 1, fresh_lb_cmds_len 1 when the trigger reply carried the command and 0 when it did not). The outcomes then follow that position and nothing else: comparison 0 holds for 1,2,3,4 (index 9: owner_cmds_len 1, proposed_cmd_op 1, trigger reply 2); comparison 1 is violated for 1,3,4,2 with complete witness 19 (owner_cmds_len 0, proposed_cmds_len 0), where the first delivered reply carried X while the trigger reply did not, so a command-carrying reply present when the trigger fires does not protect the command and the empty reply need not arrive first; comparison 2 is violated for 3,4,1,2 with complete witness 29, where both command-carrying replies are delivered after the trigger and the instance stays empty although there are now as many command-carrying as empty peer replies in the set; and comparison 3 holds for 3,1,4,2 (index 39: owner_cmds_len 1, trigger reply 1) although the first delivered reply carried nothing and the empty replies outnumber the command-carrying one in the queue before the trigger. The reply set is fixed across the four runs, so the number of command-carrying replies does not decide the outcome: the trigger prefix holds the recoverer's own reply plus two peer replies, and the owner's command survives exactly when the second peer reply carries it. The three-order tie receipt that left half the permutation space open is now completed (receipt 2ba5ed477d854a01adbca361e9a8a918, fixed experiment 1479f8725fce4b139838cfa202f7a2a1-experiment, test TestAssuranceEPaxosRecoverySameBallotOrder, exit 0, 42 parsed events, no diagnostics): with the same reply set as the earlier tie runs, the orders 2,3,4 and 4,3,2 put an empty reply at the trigger position and lose the command (comparison 0 violated with complete witness 27; comparison 2 violated with complete witness 41), while 4,2,3 puts the command-carrying reply there after an empty first delivery and keeps it (comparison 1 holds, evaluated 34). Together with the three orders of the earlier receipt, all six permutations of this reply set follow the trigger position - 2,4,3, 3,4,2, 2,3,4 and 4,3,2 drop the command, 3,2,4 and 4,2,3 keep it - so the completed permutation space contains no order that contradicts the mechanism.
counterevidence: The replacement needs a reply that carries no command at a value ballot at least as high as the recovering replica's candidate ballot; in this run that reply came from an acceptor that never pre-accepted, which required the accept broadcast to skip a failed peer, so the same reachability limit as the value-adoption finding applies.

The owner's command is not re-offered by the captured package in this scenario, and that is now measured rather than derived: receipt 098ab4425325464192aa558be557f0ce shows the decided instance holding an empty command list, the pending proposal count at 1 and nothing on the owner's propose channel, so the client-visible completion depends on the client's own retry rather than on the re-offer path that covers the single-NOOP case.

The outcome is order-dependent rather than inevitable: the third recorded order (3,2,4) kept the owner's command with the same reply set, so the empty-command loss is contingent on which reply is adopted last before the quorum trigger, not a property of the replies' content alone.

All recorded runs of the order variant come from one construction and one configuration (the pre-accept wave and the accept wave are both Thrifty subsets, so two peers hold the command and two hold nothing); the four-order receipt repeats that construction rather than reproducing the replacement in an independent scenario.

The measurement is bounded to the owner-as-recoverer case with one pending proposal; it does not show what a client library would do next, since no client process ran and the reply writer stayed empty.

The earlier claim that the two first runs refuted order dependence is withdrawn: those runs did not apply an order at all, and the order receipts show the opposite - the same message set yields two different decided commands depending only on which reply occupies the trigger position.

The loss is still a specific interleaving: it requires an empty reply to be the second delivered peer reply, and the four orders were chosen by the harness rather than sampled from a network, so the runs show that the outcome is fixed by that position and not how often such an interleaving occurs.

The completed permutation space is one reply set in one configuration: the trigger falls on the second delivered peer reply only because the recoverer's own fabricated reply counts toward SlowQuorumSize, and no run varies that quorum or uses a reply set whose value ballots differ.
limitations: One configuration and instance (N=5, F=2, instance (0,0), one command, owner as recoverer); the scenario was not repeated with a non-owner recoverer or with several commands in a batch.

The empty-command decision's execution-side effects (execution as a no-op because the batch is non-nil but empty, ordering of dependents) remain derived from source; no executor ran. The client-side effect is now measured for this scenario, including the absence of a re-offer and the empty reply writer.

The decoding behaviour is stated for the PrepareReply decoder that this path uses; the claim that all RPC decoders allocate the slice the same way rests on the generated Marshal/Unmarshal pattern rather than on a run.

The kept runs end with the instance at PREACCEPTED and the owner's command re-proposed rather than with an accepted value, and the losing runs end at PREACCEPTED with an empty batch; what a deciding quorum of the restarted phase 1 then does is outside this probe, which stops before any later round is driven.

Delivery order is measured with all six permutations of the three-reply set (2,4,3; 3,4,2; 3,2,4; 2,3,4; 4,2,3; 4,3,2) and four orders of the four-reply set (1,2,3,4; 1,3,4,2; 3,4,1,2; 3,1,4,2); the trigger position is observed directly (the delivery whose delivery replaces the bookkeeping object) rather than derived, and it is the same second reply in every recorded run.
interpretations.joint_history: The four receipts cited here belong to the same probe construction and the same configuration (N=5, F=2, instance (0,0), one command, owner as recoverer), and each index is read inside its own receipt: 81a44ff62122417db3cc5697fc5303f6 index 0 the owner's pre-recovery state, index 3 the empty acceptor, index 4 the bookkeeping after the recovery replies, index 5 the first run's outcome and indices 9-11 the same for its second run; 098ab4425325464192aa558be557f0ce indices 0 and 2-4 the client-facing run whose decided instance holds an empty command list; e89ecb076e8d4a78b174f848562ed77f indices 6, 13 and 20 the three delivery orders of the three-reply set; and 251562364ca64b3c80cd14e0d6aeddc3 indices 5, 15, 25 and 35 the observed trigger delivery of the four four-reply orders with indices 9, 19, 29 and 39 their outcomes. The newly bound experiment e25f403842234594881914f730efff4e-experiment is the revision that added the observed trigger and the four orders; it changes no handler and no scenario parameter used by the earlier receipts. The receipt 2ba5ed477d854a01adbca361e9a8a918 extends the same tie construction to the three remaining permutations; each index is read inside its own receipt (27, 34 and 41 are that receipt's run outcomes for the orders 2,3,4; 4,2,3 and 4,3,2).
